authoredSolutions.7: Diamagnetism arises from the change induced in the orbital motion of the electrons by the applied field, not from the alignment of pre-existing permanent dipoles. Since there is no permanent moment for thermal agitation to disturb, the diamagnetic susceptibility is essentially independent of temperature, unlike paramagnetism and ferromagnetism which follow \(\chi \propto \dfrac{1}{T}\). Statement I is therefore incorrect. By Lenz's law the induced moment always opposes the change that produced it, so the moment induced in a diamagnetic sample is always directed opposite to the magnetizing field, which also explains the negative susceptibility and the weak repulsion of a diamagnet out of a field. Statement II is therefore true, and the correct choice is A.
authoredSolutions.19: Escape velocity is \(v_{e} = \sqrt{\dfrac{2GM}{R}}\), so \(v_{e} \propto \sqrt{\dfrac{M}{R}}\). \[\frac{v_{planet}}{v_{earth}} = \sqrt{\frac{M_{p}}{M_{e}} \cdot \frac{R_{e}}{R_{p}}} = \sqrt{16 \times \frac{1}{4}} = \sqrt{4} = 2\] The ratio is therefore \(2:1\). [Source answer-key error: the booklet prints the ratio as 4:1, but its own worked solution ends "= 2(V escape for Earth)", which is the value used here.]
authoredSolutions.31: The substrate drawn is 4-bromopentan-2-one, \(CH_{3}COCH_{2}CH(CH_{3})Br\). Magnesium inserts into the C-Br bond, but a Grignard reagent cannot coexist with a ketone carbonyl in the same solution. Intramolecular attack of the C4 carbanion on the C2 carbonyl would close a strained three-membered ring, so the carbanion instead attacks the carbonyl carbon of a second, still unreacted molecule of the halo-ketone. The magnesium alkoxide produced is protonated by water to give the tertiary alcohol \(CH_{3}CO-CH_{2}-CH(CH_{3})-C(OH)(CH_{3})-CH_{2}-CH(CH_{3})Br\), exactly the structure of option D. Option A is only the intermediate Grignard reagent (it would be destroyed by water), option B is the disfavoured strained cyclopropanol from intramolecular addition, and option C is a geminal diol which cannot be formed here.

Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.

An N-nitrosoammonium salt is what a tertiary ALIPHATIC amine gives, and an N-nitrosoamine is what a SECONDARY amine gives; neither is formed here, so statement B is the incorrect one.

authoredSolutions.40: In an Ellingham diagram the slope of a line is \(-\Delta S\) for the oxidation reaction, so a sharp break in slope signals a sudden change in entropy. For magnesium the break near \(1120^{\circ}C\) is at the boiling point of the metal: below it the reaction is \(2Mg(l) + O_{2}(g) \rightarrow 2MgO(s)\), above it the reactant is \(Mg(g)\), and converting two moles of liquid into gas adds a large positive entropy to the reactant side. The entropy change of the reaction therefore becomes much more negative and the line turns steeply upward. Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.

authoredSolutions.44: A is squaric acid, 3,4-dihydroxycyclobut-3-ene-1,2-dione. Two equivalents of hydroxide remove both acidic protons and give the squarate dianion B. In that dianion the two negative charges and the two carbonyl groups are completely delocalised around the four-membered ring, which is planar and cyclic with two delocalised pi electrons, satisfying the \(4n + 2\) rule with \(n = 0\); so B is aromatic (statement A true) and all four ring C-C bonds become identical in length (statement D true). Statement C is true because the enediol unit of A is in equilibrium with its keto form, so A shows tautomerism. Statement B is false: squaric acid is a very strong diprotic acid (both \(pK_{a}\) values are low precisely because the dianion is aromatic), so neutralisation by hydroxide is essentially instantaneous, not slow. authoredSolutions.48: The substrate in the figure is octane-2,7-dione, \(CH_{3}CO(CH_{2})_{4}COCH_{3}\). Option D is the seven-membered minor product and options A and B are intermolecular condensation products.
authoredSolutions.49: (A) Electron deficient hydrides come from group 13, where the central atom has fewer electrons than needed for normal two-centre bonds; \(B_{2}H_{6}\), with its three-centre two-electron banana bonds, is the standard example, so A-III. (C) Electron precise hydrides come from group 14 and have exactly the electrons needed for the bonds drawn; \(CH_{4}\) is tetrahedral and precise, so C-IV. (D) Saline (ionic) hydrides are formed by the strongly electropositive s-block metals; \(MgH_{2}\) is the only such compound listed, so D-I. The match is A-III, B-II, C-IV, D-I.

authoredSolutions.51: For an isothermal reversible expansion of an ideal gas the internal energy does not change, so the heat absorbed by the gas equals the work it does: \(q_{rev} = nRT\ln(V_{2}/V_{1}) = 1 \times 8.314 \times 350 \times \ln(3.0/2.0) = 1180\) J. This heat is drawn reversibly from the surroundings, which therefore lose exactly that much heat at 350 K. Hence \(\Delta S_{surr} = -q_{rev}/T = -1180/350 = -3.37\) J per K, whose magnitude to the nearest integer is 3.
authoredSolutions.52: Cyclohexanecarbaldehyde is \(C_{6}H_{11}CHO\), that is \(C_{7}H_{12}O\), of molar mass \(84 + 12 + 16 = 112\) g/mol, so 131.8 kg is \(131.8/112 = 1.177\) kmol. authoredSolutions.53: Alanylglycylphenylalanylisoleucine is the tetrapeptide Ala-Gly-Phe-Ile.
